headings.title: Introduction to Internally Displaced Persons (IDPs)
headings.content: Internally Displaced Persons (IDPs) are individuals or groups who have been forced or obliged to flee or to leave their homes or places of habitual residence, in particular as a result of or in order to avoid the effects of armed conflict, situations of generalized violence, violations of human rights or natural or human-made disasters, and who have not crossed an internationally recognized State border. Unlike refugees who cross international borders and fall under specific international legal protections, IDPs remain within their own country and technically remain under the protection of their national government. For nursing students in Nigeria, understanding this distinction is crucial because the responsibility for IDP welfare lies heavily with national and local health authorities, non-governmental organizations, and domestic disaster management agencies like the National Emergency Management Agency (NEMA). Nigeria has experienced significant internal displacement due to various factors, particularly in the North-East region with the Boko Haram insurgency, banditry in the North-West and North-Central zones, and communal clashes, as well as seasonal flooding across the country. As future community health nurses, you will encounter IDP populations living in formal camps, informal settlements, or integrated within host communities. Recognizing their legal status and the root causes of their displacement helps in planning culturally sensitive, context-appropriate nursing interventions. IDPs often face severe disruptions in social structures, loss of livelihoods, and acute vulnerabilities that demand comprehensive healthcare delivery. Nurses play a frontline role in advocacy, disease surveillance, and direct clinical care to mitigate the adverse health outcomes associated with displacement.

headings.title: Causes and Drivers of Internal Displacement in Nigeria
headings.content: Internal displacement in Nigeria is driven by a complex interplay of security, environmental, and socio-economic factors. Armed conflict and generalized violence constitute the most prominent drivers, notably the prolonged insurgency in the North-East involving Boko Haram and Islamic State's West Africa Province (ISWAP). This conflict has destroyed infrastructure, burned villages, and forced millions to flee their ancestral homes. Additionally, protracted farmer-herder conflicts and escalating banditry across the North-West and North-Central regions have displaced rural farming communities, severely threatening food security and regional stability. Environmental factors also play a critical role; climate change has accelerated desertification in the far North and triggered devastating annual riverine and flash floods across various Nigerian states, displacing entire communities and destroying livelihoods. Furthermore, developmental projects, communal clashes, and ethnic tensions occasionally force populations to relocate internally. As nursing professionals, analyzing these root causes helps contextualize the trauma, physical injuries, and socio-economic destitution experienced by arriving populations. Understanding the specific driver of displacement in a given community allows nurses to anticipate unique health threats—such as trauma and gunshot wounds from insurgent violence versus waterborne diseases from flooding—thereby guiding targeted preventive and curative nursing care in temporary settlements.

headings.title: Vulnerabilities and Special Health Needs of IDPs
headings.content: Displacement drastically amplifies pre-existing health vulnerabilities while creating new, acute risks, particularly for vulnerable groups such as women, children, the elderly, and individuals with chronic illnesses or disabilities. Pregnant and lactating women face severe risks due to the collapse of antenatal care services, leading to high rates of complicated deliveries, maternal morbidity, and neonatal mortality. Children under five are disproportionately affected by acute malnutrition, vaccine-preventable diseases, and severe dehydration from diarrheal illnesses due to poor sanitation in overcrowded camps. The elderly often suffer from neglected chronic conditions such as hypertension and diabetes, exacerbated by a lack of continuous medication and the stress of displacement. Furthermore, IDP camps and informal settlements are high-risk environments for gender-based violence (GBV), sexual exploitation, and abuse, driven by lack of privacy, poor lighting, and scarce resources. Persons with disabilities face physical barriers in navigating camp infrastructure and often struggle to access food distribution lines or emergency exits. Community health nurses must prioritize these vulnerable groups during assessments and routine clinics. Tailored interventions, such as establishing safe spaces for women, ensuring targeted supplementary feeding for infants, and creating accessible healthcare pathways, are vital to safeguarding the health and dignity of displaced populations.

headings.title: Public Health Challenges in IDP Camps
headings.content: The living conditions in IDP camps and host communities frequently give rise to severe public health challenges. Overcrowding, inadequate shelter, and substandard living spaces facilitate the rapid transmission of airborne and droplet infections such as measles, meningitis, and acute respiratory infections. Water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) inadequacies are major public health hazards; contaminated water sources and open defecation lead to outbreaks of waterborne diseases like cholera, typhoid fever, and hepatitis E. Vector-borne diseases such as malaria also surge due to poor drainage, stagnant water, and insufficient distribution of insecticide-treated bed nets. Nutritional deficiencies are widespread, with acute food insecurity manifesting as severe acute malnutrition (SAM) and moderate acute malnutrition (MAM) among children and pregnant women. Additionally, limited access to healthcare facilities and interrupted supply chains for essential medicines delay diagnosis and treatment. Communicable disease surveillance systems are often weak or absent in newly established camps, delaying outbreak detection and response. Community health nurses must implement active epidemiological surveillance, promote health education regarding hygiene practices, collaborate with environmental health officers to monitor water safety, and ensure early case identification to curb potential epidemics within displaced communities.

headings.title: Community Health Nursing Assessment for IDPs
headings.content: Conducting a comprehensive community health nursing assessment among IDPs requires a systematic, culturally sensitive approach to identify immediate health threats and community assets. The nursing assessment begins with a rapid epidemiological appraisal to determine camp demographics, population size, distribution of vulnerable groups, and prevailing morbidity and mortality patterns. Nurses must assess environmental health conditions, including the safety of drinking water sources, latrine-to-population ratios, waste disposal mechanisms, and food storage facilities. Clinical assessments focus on identifying active disease outbreaks, nutritional status using mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC) tapes for children, and the availability of maternal and child health services. Furthermore, psychosocial assessments are essential to gauge trauma levels, stress-related disorders, and coping mechanisms within the displaced community. In conducting these assessments, nurses must engage community leaders, youth representatives, and traditional birth attendants to build trust and ensure active participation. Data gathered during the assessment phase guides the prioritization of nursing diagnoses, such as risk for infection, imbalanced nutrition, and post-trauma syndrome. By partnering with the displaced population rather than imposing external solutions, community health nurses ensure that subsequent care plans are practical, acceptable, and effective in meeting real needs.

headings.title: Primary Health Care and Management Strategies in Camps
headings.content: Primary Health Care (PHC) serves as the cornerstone for managing health crises in IDP settlements, focusing on accessible, equitable, and community-based interventions. The management strategy in camps involves establishing temporary health posts or mobile clinics that deliver the minimum initial service package (MISP) for reproductive health, routine immunization, and management of common morbidities like malaria, respiratory infections, and diarrhea. Nurses play a pivotal role in organizing triage systems, providing curative consultations under standing orders, and dispensing essential medications from the WHO essential drug list. Disease surveillance is integrated into daily PHC operations using early warning outbreak response systems to detect anomalies such as sudden spikes in watery diarrhea or fever. In addition to curative care, health promotion and disease prevention are aggressively pursued through community health education campaigns on hand hygiene, safe water storage, and vector control. Collaboration with nutrition stabilization centers ensures that children identified with severe acute malnutrition with medical complications are promptly referred for inpatient therapeutic care. Effective PHC management in IDP settings also requires establishing functional referral pathways to secondary and tertiary health facilities for emergency obstetric care, surgical interventions, and specialized management, ensuring continuity of care despite displacement.

headings.title: Psychosocial Support and Mental Health Care for Displaced Populations
headings.content: Displacement is profoundly traumatic, exposing individuals to violence, loss of loved ones, destruction of property, and severe uncertainty about the future. Consequently, mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS) is an indispensable component of comprehensive nursing care for IDPs. Displaced populations frequently exhibit symptoms of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), anxiety, severe depression, grief, and adjustment disorders. Children may manifest behavioral regressions, enuresis, and school avoidance, while adults may resort to harmful coping mechanisms such as substance abuse. Community health nurses must provide psychological first aid (PFA) upon arrival, which involves offering practical care, assessing needs, listening without forcing talk, and connecting survivors with available support services. Nurses should also facilitate community-based psychosocial activities, support groups, and safe recreational spaces for children to restore a sense of normalcy and social cohesion. For individuals with severe psychiatric conditions, nurses coordinate referral pathways to visiting psychiatrists or psychiatric nurses for specialized pharmacological management and counseling. Integrating mental health care into routine camp clinics reduces social stigmatization, encourages treatment-seeking behavior, and promotes holistic healing and resilience among trauma survivors.

headings.title: Multi-Sectoral Collaboration and Policy Frameworks for IDP Care
headings.content: Addressing the complex health and social needs of Internally Displaced Persons exceeds the capacity of any single health agency or nursing department, necessitating robust multi-sectoral collaboration. Effective IDP care involves coordinated partnerships between governmental bodies (such as State Emergency Management Agencies and Ministries of Health), international organizations (like UNHCR, UNICEF, and WHO), local and international non-governmental organizations (NGOs), faith-based organizations, and community leadership structures. Within this multi-sectoral framework, nurses collaborate with WASH engineers to ensure clean water supply, nutritionists for food distribution, security personnel for camp safety, and social workers for child protection and tracing missing family members. At the policy level, nurses must be familiar with international guidelines such as the Kampala Convention (African Union Convention for the Protection and Assistance of Internally Displaced Persons in Africa) and national IDP policies that guarantee the rights of displaced citizens to healthcare, shelter, and security. Advocacy by nursing associations ensures that health remains a central agenda in humanitarian response plans. By understanding these policy frameworks and collaborative networks, nursing students learn to coordinate referrals, share epidemiological data across agencies, and advocate for sustainable solutions—such as voluntary, safe, and dignified return, local integration, or resettlement—thereby contributing meaningfully to national health security and humanitarian relief.
